source.title: Unifying Learning Dynamics and Generalization in Transformers Scaling Law

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figure text is garbled in the extracted text; the tables and main reported results remain readable.
record.tranche_reason: It develops a theoretical scaling account and tests qualitative scaling predictions using validation cross-entropy sweeps, rather than reproducing the original empirical procedures. Its results also qualify the proposed scaling shapes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports empirical scaling fits, loss trends, a compute-frontier fit, and noise-sweep outcomes. Theoretical bounds and findings cited from other studies are not recorded as empirical rows. Figure-only GPT-2 curves do not provide extractable numerical values; their textual trends are recorded in aggregate rows. The paper does not test prediction of larger runs from fits on smaller runs, a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape sensitivity at fixed parameter count, or downstream-task predictability.
record.test_reason: All experiments continue training pretrained GPT-2 and Pythia checkpoints on TinyStories and WikiText-103. None trains from scratch. The empirical results therefore bear on V5 (the power-law form in fine-tuning) and on V7 (single power-law and additive forms fail or bend), not on V1's pretraining-loss claim. The paper's main contribution is theoretical: an NTK-regime two-stage excess-risk bound. The experiments are explicitly framed as qualitative validation only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive a two-stage excess-risk bound (exponential in compute, then Θ(C^-1/7)) for lazy-regime transformers trained on squared loss. Their GPT-2 and Pythia fine-tuning experiments are presented as qualitative validation of the transition and of noise-driven breakdown of data scaling. They state the Pythia joint-fit exponents are in the range of Chinchilla's. They explicitly retract quantitative claims about the elbow and the exact exponent.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical transformer-kernel analysis plus qualitative scaling sweeps, rather than the original empirical scaling-law fitting and compute-optimal allocation methodology. Experiments fine-tune GPT-2 and pretrained Pythia models and do not test small-run extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model/data interaction, noise schedule, and corruption type. The Pythia joint fit uses a monotonicity criterion and excludes six LR-mistuned cells; the compute frontier uses a running minimum; the trajectory exponent depends on fitting the early quartile versus late half. GPT-2 settings use cosine decay and warmup; Pythia uses size-specific learning rates and cosine schedules.

fits_no_version.finding: With deliberately corrupted fine-tuning data, the gain from adding data depends on how the corruption rate grows. Under GPT-2 M2, the gap to clean stalls at +0.29–0.30 while absolute loss still falls. Under Pythia M2ext with mask-token corruption, the gap flattens (+1.27→+1.07). Under M3, and under M2ext with random tokens, the gap grows, and absolute loss at 16M exceeds 4M (e.g. 4.06 vs 3.98).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data scaling of LM loss stalls or reverses when added data carries noise whose variance grows about linearly or faster with dataset size.

record.problems: The authors state that their theorem bounds squared excess risk while experiments use cross-entropy and validate only qualitative predictions. The compute-transition elbow is not identifiable; GPT-2 provides only four sizes per data value and four data values, and per-run uncertainty is not separately reported. The Pythia fit excludes six cells for apparent learning-rate mistuning, has an N × D interaction, and its reported clean 12M baseline is interpolated. No seed-level uncertainty is reported for the loss tables or trajectory exponent.
record.rows_left_out: Exact values from the supplementary GPT-2 model/data/time curves in Figures 6–9 are not extractable from the figure text; the reported qualitative trends are summarized in r1. No results-bearing numerical rows were omitted from the readable tables.

untested.parts: No pretraining-from-scratch runs. All experiments continue training pretrained checkpoints on new corpora.
No compute-optimal N/D allocation estimated. The theory's M∝N³ is explicitly not a compute-optimal recommendation.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated-data scaling and transfer are not tested. Only one LM fine-tuning setting per model family.
No systematic variation of parameter counting, schedule or fitting method. Published exponents are not compared beyond a range statement.

missing.what: In the joint fit, E was constrained to [1.5, 3.0], and the estimate (1.50) sits at the lower bound. This bears on fit-dependence of α and β.
missing.locator: Appendix C.3, Joint Hoffmann fit; Table 3

missing.what: Epoch budget varies by data slice ({6,6,6,6,3,2,2} passes), so smaller-D cells involve repeated data. The peak LR is also size-specific. Both confound the data-scaling fit.
Authors explicitly retract any quantitative claim about the elbow location and the −1/7 value.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 links were removed: every run starts from a pretrained checkpoint (fine-tuning/SFT), so the results bear on V5, not on pretraining loss. The noise sweeps induce corruption deliberately and test the paper's own breakdown prediction, so they go to fits_no_version. Clean-data rows r6–r9 and r22–r25 serve as baselines and are linked to V5 only as a series. The theoretical results (bounds, the Lambert-W numerical figure) are not empirical and are not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Empirical validation cross-entropy is examined, but the experiments are qualitative and do not establish power laws over several orders of magnitude for every variable. The theoretical result concerns squared excess risk, not ordinary language-model cross-entropy.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of substantially larger runs.
No loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is estimated as a function of fixed compute; equal-compute comparisons do not establish stable allocation exponents.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
A Pythia SFT sweep tests scaling across model and data sizes in one fine-tuning setting. Other modalities, repeated data, and other training regimes are not tested.

The results show a fitted exponent differing from the theoretical exponent and an interaction not captured by the additive fit; they do not systematically vary fitting choices or establish that published exponents disagree because of specific choices.

rows.subject: Pythia × WikiText-103
rows.stage_stated: SFT from publicly released pretrained checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Fit a joint model-size/data-size loss curve to the Pythia sweep.

conditions.value: L(N,D) = E + AN^-α + BD^-β; log-space MSE; 36 cells retained
Six cells excluded for terminal loss exceeding the running minimum by more than 0.05 nats

rows.measure: Validation cross-entropy joint-fit exponents and fit quality
rows.uncertainty: 400-sample bootstrap 95% CIs: α [0.339, 0.689]; β [0.153, 0.940]; E [1.50, 1.84]. R²log = 0.851 and log-RMSE = 0.101 are also reported.
rows.note: The additive fit is described as reasonable at this scale, but the remaining error reflects an N × D interaction: small models drop about 2.85 nats across the data range, while models ≥1.4B drop about 0.30 nats.
rows.check: V1 removed (SFT setting). The additive fit gives R²log 0.85, but there is a strong N×D interaction: 70M drops about 2.85 nats versus about 0.30 for models of 1.4B and above. E sits at its constraint bound (1.50, constrained to [1.5,3.0]). Six cells were excluded. Bootstrap CIs are wide and include the Chinchilla α and β.

rows.note: The paper describes this as qualitatively near the theoretical 1/7 ≈ 0.143, with exponent identification only qualitative at this scale.

rows.measure: Validation cross-entropy versus compute; late-half power-law exponent and fit crossover

rows.note: The exponent is shallower than the theoretical −1/7 ≈ −0.143; the paper presents this as qualitative evidence for the transition, not a precise exponent match.
rows.check: V1 removed. This is a single Pythia-70M trajectory, with about 1.3 post-warmup decades of compute. An exponential fit (early quartile) and a power-law fit (late half, η=0.087) are each fitted separately, with no model comparison.

relationships.condition: Pythia 70M–2.8B SFT on WikiText-103; GPT-2 124M–1.5B fine-tuning on TinyStories
relationships.reason: Power-law fits in fine-tuning: joint fit α=0.428, β=0.337 (R²log 0.851); compute frontier η=0.120. GPT-2 curves are described as consistent with Kaplan (r1, r3, r4).
relationships.display_finding: Pythia's joint fit has α = 0.428, β = 0.337, and log-space R² = 0.851, with compute-frontier η = 0.120, while GPT-2 curves are described as consistent with Kaplan scaling.

relationships.condition: Pythia SFT joint fit and single-trajectory fit
relationships.reason: The additive form misses a strong N×D interaction (2.85 vs 0.30 nats drop). E hits its constraint bound and six cells were excluded. Exponents differ by measure (late-trajectory 0.087 vs frontier 0.120) (r3, r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: The additive fit missed a model–data interaction associated with 2.85 versus 0.30 nats of loss reduction, E reached its constraint bound, and late-trajectory and frontier exponents differed at 0.087 versus 0.120.

relationships.condition: Pythia-70M trajectory and Pythia joint fit; GPT-2 equal-FLOPs comparisons (qualitative only)
relationships.reason: The loss trajectory is fit by an early exponential and a late power law. The additive power-law form leaves a structural N×D residual. The equal-compute regime switch suggests a bend, though no model comparison is done and the elbow is not identifiable (r2, r3, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Pythia-70M loss was fit by an early exponential and late power law, the joint Pythia additive power-law fit left a systematic model-size–data interaction residual, and qualitative GPT-2 equal-compute comparisons suggested a regime bend without identifying an elbow or comparing alternative models.
